prize_parts.citation: for establishing the role of nominal rigidities in macroeconomics, through staggered price setting and wage contracts, interest-rate policy rules and a micro-founded framework for the analysis of monetary policy

statement.case_for: The New Keynesian framework is a scientific advance and also changed practice. Calvo's time-dependent pricing and Taylor's staggered contracts supply the nominal-rigidity primitives. Taylor's rule turned policy conduct into an estimable relationship. Woodford integrated these into a micro-founded theory of interest and prices with an explicit welfare criterion. The result is a framework in which the transmission of policy can be analysed, estimated and communicated. This matches the criterion I care most about: a specific scientific contribution with big, durable consequences, not a lifetime-achievement judgement. It has also had decades of testing, including the 2008 crisis, the zero lower bound and the 2021-23 inflation. That testing prompted criticism and refinement, but the core apparatus remains the common language of the field. Of the shortlisted candidates, I find the combination of originality, breadth and durability strongest here. The attribution is hard but workable, because the three named contributions are distinct and each is identifiable in a specific body of work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. At least six or seven contributors have serious claims (Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler, Smets and others), and any three-person cap leaves out work that made the framework estimable and usable in practice. A second reservation concerns what the prize would be rewarding. The framework's performance after the financial crisis and during the post-pandemic inflation is contested, and heterogeneous-agent extensions may be seen as its successor. Earlier prizes to Lucas, Sargent, Sims and Bernanke also cover adjacent ground. I rely on my own knowledge of the literature for the priority claims and have not verified them independently.

responses.point: Fredriksson proposes Woodford, Gali and Taylor, arguing that this trio covers the conceptual, empirical and policy-rule contributions, and he acknowledges that omitting Calvo, Gertler and the Christiano-Eichenbaum group is a real cost.
responses.response: I agree the exclusions are costly, and I think Gali has a serious claim. I still keep Calvo over Gali because Calvo's pricing mechanism is the primitive on which the New Keynesian Phillips curve is built. Gali's work is mainly development, empirical grounding and extension of that primitive, which is valuable but a step downstream. If the committee wants to weight empirical validation and the estimated-model tradition more heavily, then Gali in place of Calvo is the natural swap, and I would not object strongly. I base this on the structure of the contributions and not on how many colleagues name each person.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B003 first. He argues that Kiyotaki-Moore and Gertler's intermediary work give a foundational account of how credit constraints amplify shocks, and that the 2022 prize makes this a related rather than duplicative recognition.
responses.response: I accept that Kiyotaki-Moore is an original and cleanly attributable mechanism, and on attribution it is easier than B014. My reservations are two. First, the original contribution has thin direct empirical identification, and the evidence for the mechanism came mostly from later work. Second, Gertler is cross-listed in B014 and the financial-accelerator line is adjacent to the 2022 award, which narrows the marginal space. I therefore keep it below B014 on breadth of influence over practice, though I regard it as a legitimate candidate. I do not think its relative standing should be settled by the fact that its attribution is tidier.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B047 first. He argues that Melitz (2003) is a central and unambiguous contribution that moved trade analysis from industries to firms, that Helpman adds breadth, and that the framework has more than two decades of confirmation.
responses.response: I largely agree on attribution and maturity. Melitz is unambiguous, trade has not been recognised since 2008, and this is why I rank B047 second and name it as an alternative. Where I differ is on ordering. The influence of B014 on the conduct of policy, and not just on research, seems to me larger, and the Melitz framework is a refinement of firm-level trade after the new trade theory recognised in 2008. I also share your concern about priority relative to Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, who are not on the ballot entry, and about whether Helpman is rewarded for this framework or for his wider body of work.

uncertainties: Whether the third name should be Calvo or Gali, and whether a narrower citation focused on pricing frictions would resolve the attribution problem.
How much the committee weights the framework's mixed performance in the post-2021 inflation episode and the heterogeneous-agent critique.
Whether adjacent macro prizes (Lucas, Sargent and Sims, Kydland and Prescott, Bernanke) reduce the marginal case for monetary macroeconomics.
Priority and the precise division of credit among the contributors are based on my own knowledge of the literature and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My field (labour economics and crime) is closest to B046 and B045, which I rank below my preferred configuration.
